title: Bits: Counting Bits for 0 to n
oneLiner: Return the number of 1 bits in every number from 0 to n in one O(n) pass, reusing the answer for i >> 1.
keyTakeaway: i >> 1 is i with its lowest bit dropped, and it's smaller than i, so its count is already known: bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1). That turns n separate popcounts into a one-line dynamic programming fill, O(n) total. The same idea works with i & (i - 1), which clears the lowest set bit: bits[i] = bits[i & (i - 1)] + 1.
explanation:
Given n, return an array ans of length n + 1 where ans[i] is the number of 1 bits in the binary form of i (its popcount, short for population count). For n = 5: 0, 1, 10, 11, 100, 101 have 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2 ones, so the answer is [0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2].

Counting each number's bits separately (the Count Set Bits lesson in the Patterns track) costs about log n per number, O(n log n) in total. You can do better by reusing earlier answers, which is dynamic programming on bits.

Shifting right by one, i >> 1, throws away the lowest bit: 13 is 1101, and 13 >> 1 is 110, which is 6. So 13 has the same 1 bits as 6, plus one more if its lowest bit was 1. The lowest bit is i & 1 (AND with 1 keeps only that bit). Since i >> 1 is smaller than i, ans[i >> 1] is already filled in when you get to i: ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1). One pass from 1 to n, constant work each.

Second recurrence, same speed: i & (i - 1) is i with its LOWEST SET bit cleared (subtracting 1 turns the lowest 1 into 0 and every 0 below it into 1, so the AND wipes exactly that bit). That number is smaller and has exactly one fewer 1, so ans[i] = ans[i & (i - 1)] + 1.

Built-ins, for when you only need one count: BitOperations.PopCount((uint)x) in System.Numerics, or int.PopCount(x) in .NET 7 and later; x.bit_count() in Python 3.10 and later, or bin(x).count("1") before that. Note that bin() of a negative Python int is "-0b101", the sign and magnitude, not a two's complement bit pattern, so its 1s are not the 32-bit popcount. Mask with x & 0xFFFFFFFF first.

The visualization fills ans for n = 8.

visualizationSteps.message: n = 8. ans[0] = 0 (0 has no 1 bits). Index i of the array is the number i.
i = 1 (1). i >> 1 = 0 (0) already has 0; the dropped lowest bit i & 1 = 1. ans[1] = 0 + 1 = 1.
i = 2 (10). i >> 1 = 1 (1) already has 1; the dropped lowest bit i & 1 = 0. ans[2] = 1 + 0 = 1.
i = 3 (11). i >> 1 = 1 (1) already has 1; the dropped lowest bit i & 1 = 1. ans[3] = 1 + 1 = 2.
i = 4 (100). i >> 1 = 2 (10) already has 1; the dropped lowest bit i & 1 = 0. ans[4] = 1 + 0 = 1.
i = 5 (101). i >> 1 = 2 (10) already has 1; the dropped lowest bit i & 1 = 1. ans[5] = 1 + 1 = 2.
i = 6 (110). i >> 1 = 3 (11) already has 2; the dropped lowest bit i & 1 = 0. ans[6] = 2 + 0 = 2.
i = 7 (111). i >> 1 = 3 (11) already has 2; the dropped lowest bit i & 1 = 1. ans[7] = 2 + 1 = 3.
i = 8 (1000). i >> 1 = 4 (100) already has 1; the dropped lowest bit i & 1 = 0. ans[8] = 1 + 0 = 1.
Done: [0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1], one O(1) step per number.

recognitionSignals: A per-bit property (popcount, parity) needed for EVERY number in a range, not just one.
"Can you do it in O(n) without a built-in?": reuse the answer for a smaller number with one bit removed.
A number's answer depends on the same number with one bit removed: a DP over i >> 1 or i & (i - 1).
gotchas: The result has n + 1 entries, from 0 to n inclusive.
Write (i >> 1) and (i & 1) with brackets: in C# and Python, + binds tighter than >> and &, so ans[i >> 1] + i & 1 parses as (ans[i >> 1] + i) & 1.
In Python, bin(-5).count('1') counts the bits of 5, not the 32-bit two's complement pattern of -5.
confusableWith: Bit Manipulation: Count Set Bits (Patterns track) counts ONE number's bits by shifting; this lesson needs all of 0..n and reuses earlier answers.
Climbing Stairs and other 1-D DP fill an array left to right from earlier cells; here the earlier cell is i >> 1 instead of i - 1.

complexity.note: One O(1) step per number from 0 to n. The output array is n + 1 long; nothing else is allocated.
